Title: A Practical Application of Management and Organization Theory for Academic Administrator.
Abstract: In this article the author examines the communication gap the exists between practitioners and theorists in the management and organizational fields and attempts to bridge this divide. He presents his case in hopes of demonstrating to academic administrators that having a recognition of management and organizational principals can be invaluable when managing change. He notes that being aware of these principals can help change come about more smoothly and achieve desired results more quickly. He presents a case that outlines how the application of ineffective management principals can slow the process of organizational change and present unnecessary problems for those in charge of implementing the change.

Title: A Practical Application of Management and Organization Theory for the Academic Administrator
Affiliations: Saint Louis University
Abstract: In this article the author examines the communication gap the exists between practitioners and theorists in the management and organizational fields and attempts to bridge this divide. He presents his case in hopes of demonstrating to academic administrators that having a recognition of management and organizational principals can be invaluable when managing change. He notes that being aware of these principals can help change come about more smoothly and achieve desired results more quickly. He presents a case that outlines how the application of ineffective management principals can slow the process of organizational change and present unnecessary problems for those in charge of implementing the change.

Title: The Maligned F.W. Taylor: A Reply to His Many Critics
Affiliations: Ohio State University
Abstract: In this article the author comes to the defense of the designer of the management science known as Taylorism, Frederick W. Taylor. The author traces Taylor's thinking and discusses the impact that he had on the field and addresses both those who have criticized and praised his theories. He notes that Taylor has been regarded, most notably, as being responsible for laying the foundation on which productivity in the modern economy has been improved. The author discusses the contributions that Taylor made on behalf of the worker outlining his concepts for offering incentives to employees, shortening hours of labor and improving working conditions.

Title: Classroom Techniques in Teaching by the Case Method
Affiliations: Boston University
Abstract: In this article the author outlines a method, which builds on pervious research on teaching by case method, for conducting a successful classroom discussion in a business policy course. He notes that teaching is largely an individual process; however, building a framework is important, especially for longer courses. The author outlines a three step process for establishing this framework starting with course design, class preparation and finally a method of conducting class discussions. He provides extensive details into each of these areas, essentially presenting an overview on how to conduct a class from beginning to end. He closes by noting that to effectively teach by case method the instructor must be fully prepared.

Title: The Experiential Exercise Situation: A Comment on Instructional Role and Pedagogy Evaluation
Affiliations: Indiana State University
Abstract: In this article the author examines the effectiveness of using experiential exercise learning materials in management education. He notes that in this method students actively participate in the performance of a goal-oriented task and learn both from the task itself as well as from a subsequent evaluation of the performance. He adds that the effectiveness of this method is largely attributed to the effectiveness of the instructor. He outlines a generally used role of the instructor of these methods discussing how to maximize the experiential learning effects as well as the importance of this role in the evaluation of the method.

Title: Simulation Gaming: The Confluence of Quantitative and Behavioral Theory
Authors: Henry P. Sims, Herbert H. Hand
Affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; University of South Carolina
Abstract: In this article the authors examine the effectiveness of simulation gaming in business education. They discuss previous research that has indicated that business students have not been properly prepared for the real world dimensions of their careers. In this paper they propose that simulation gaming has begun to combat this problem by allowing students to face the real world situations they can expect to encounter after school. They assert that gaming has the ability to prepare students for the environment of uncertainty that exists in real organizations. By gaining experience with techniques such as managing both people and products students can better equip themselves for the decisions they will face as managers.

Title: Productivity From Scanlon-type Plans
Affiliations: University of Otago
Abstract: In an examination of the Scanlon Plan and the factors which determine the probability of success, the economic motivation is seen as being of major importance. The assumption of psychologists that most workers desire participation in decision making, and thus self actualization, and that this produces the productivity improvement, is criticized

Title: Towards Systemic Methodology For Evaluating The Impact Of Interventions On Organizational Effectiveness.
Authors: Ralph H. Kilmann, Richard P. Herden
Abstract: A methodology is proposed by which relevant persons can systematically partake in conceptualizing which components of effectiveness are most central to an organization, how to choose evaluation methodologies to measure these components, and how to evaluate the impact of a change program to enhance the effectiveness of the organization.

Title: Towards A Systemic Methodology For Evaluating The Impact Of Interventions On Organizational Effectiveness
Authors: Ralph H. Kilmann, Richard P. Herden
Affiliations: University of Pittsburgh
Abstract: A methodology is proposed by which relevant persons can systematically partake in conceptualizing which components of effectiveness are most central to an organization, how to choose evaluation methodologies to measure these components, and how to evaluate the impact of a change program to enhance the effectiveness of the organization.

Title: Changing Toward Participative Management Approaches: A Model and Method
Affiliations: Wayne State University
Abstract: A typology of participative approaches and methods is applied to organizations. Mechanisms behind the methods are discussed; a causal model is developed; and sets of contingencies conditioning the operation of the model are described. Issues around change toward participation are defined and illustrated, centering on the issue of congruence between the change method and the specific participative approach.

Title: Seducing the Elite: The Politics of Decision Making and Innovation in Organizational Network.
Abstract: The success or failure of innovative ventures depends largely upon gaining and holding the support of organizational elites. This article presents analysis and strategies to elicit elite support initially, and develops the innovator's role in maintaining elite support for the innovation until its eventual implementation.

Title: Seducing the Elites: The Politics of Decision Making and Innovation in Organizational Network
Affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison
Abstract: The success or failure of innovative ventures depends largely upon gaining and holding the support of organizational elites. This article presents analysis and strategies to elicit elite support initially, and develops the innovator's role in maintaining elite support for the innovation until its eventual implementation.

Title: A Theoretical Synthesis of Job Performance and the Evaluative Dimension of Organizational Climate: A Social Psychological Perspective
Affiliations: University of South Carolina
Abstract: Studies linking organizational climate to job performance have been diverse and at times contradictory; however, social psychologists have dealt with a similar problem in the area of social facilitation. Social facilitation is related to the evaluative aspect of organizational climate in an effort to explain previous contradictory results.

Title: A Framework for the Comparative Analysis of Personnel Administration
Authors: V. V. Murray, Harish C. Jain, Roy J. Adams
Affiliations: York University; McMaster University
Abstract: There is a relative absence of international comparative research and theory on personnel policies and practices. A conceptual framework to facilitate cross-cultural analyses is presented noting the effects of cultural characteristics on the validity, priority ranking, feasibility and organization of the standard personnel functions. Illustrations of the framework draw on existing literature.

Title: Bureaucracy and Professionalism: A Reconsideration of Weber's Thesis
Affiliations: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
Abstract: One criticism of Weber's ideal-type of bureaucracy has been that in defining its characteristics Weber did not distinguish between hierarchical and professional authority. Critics see these as inherently in-compatible and in conflict in formal organizations. Recent empirical findings indicate that professionalism and bureaucracy may be positively related on the level of organizational structure and individual orientation. Implications for organizational theory and practice are noted.

Title: The Congruence of Factor-Analytic Structures: Comparisons of Four Procedures and Their Solutions
Authors: Robert T. Golembiewski, Keith Billingsley, Samuel Yeager
Affiliations: University of Georgia
Abstract: Use of factor analytic techniques for the analysts of organizational data is increasing. Four readily available techniques are described. Results derived from application of each technique to a common data set are compared.

Title: The Organization and Management of the Temple Corporations in Ancient Mesopotamia
Affiliations: The University of Houston
Abstract: Ancient Mesopotamians were perhaps the first people to evolve a methodical, disciplined approach to the management of large-scale, complex organizations. The success and longevity of their temple corporations provide dramatic testimony to the versatility and effectiveness of the managerial concepts and techniques which they developed.

Title: The Social Response Process in Commercial Banks: An Empirical Investigation
Affiliations: Northwestern University
Abstract: Two large commercial banks were studied in depth to document the "social response process". By tracing and comparing the development of commercial lending programs for minorities in both banks, a response process similar to that found in decentralized, divisionalized manufacturing companies was identified.

Title: Organization and Management Theory
Affiliations: Ohio State University
Abstract: This article presents reviews of several books including, “Formal Organizations: A Comparative Approach,” by P. M. Blau and W. R. Scott, “A Behavioral Theory of the Firm,” by Richard M. Cyert and James G. March and “The Casual Texture of Organizational Environments, Human Relations,” vol. 18, by F. E. Emery and E. L. Trist.

Title: Health Care Administration
Affiliations: University of Miami, Coral Gables
Abstract: This article presents reviews of several books including, “Principals of Hospital Administration,” by Jim McGibony, “The Care of Health in Communities: Access for Outcasts,” by Nancy Milio and “Introduction to Health Planning,” by D. C. Bergwall.

Title: Managerial Consultation
Affiliations: President, Management and Business Services, Columbus, Ohio
Abstract: This article presents reviews of several books including, “Intervention Theory and Method: A Behavioral Science View,” by Chris Argyris, “The External Consultant's Role in Organizational Change,” by Neil G. Davey and “Making the Most of Consulting Services,” by Jerome H. Fuchs.

Title: Personal/Human Resources
Affiliations: The University of Michigan
Abstract: This article presents reviews of several books including, “Manpower Planning and the Development of Human Resources,” by Thomas H. Patten, “Manpower Planning and Programming,” edited by E. H. Burack and J. W. Walker and “Performance in Organizations: Determinants and Appraisal,” by L. L. Cummings and D. P. Schwab.

Title: Organizational Development
Affiliations: University of Colorado, Boulder
Abstract: This article presents reviews of several books including, “The Social Technology of Organization Development,” by W. Warner Burke and Harvey A. Hornstein, “Organizational Development,” by Wendell L. French and Cecil H. Bell and “Sensitivity Training and the Laboratory Approach,” 2nd ed., by Robert T. Colembiewski and Arthur Blumberg.

Title: Organizational Communication.
Production/Operations Management.
Business Policy and Planning
Affiliations: Purdue University
Abstract: This article presents reviews of several books including, “Corporate Strategy,” by Igor Ansoff, “Business Policy: Text & Cases,” by Edmund Learned, C. Roland Christensen, Kenneth R. Andrews and Wiliam Guth and “Top Management Planning,” by George Steiner.

Title: The Death of Management — A Search for Causes
Affiliations: Virginia Commonwealth University
Abstract: In this article the author provides his opinion on why he believes the study of management is dead. He believes that the field has become to concerned with what he calls trivia and is no longer concerned with what is actually taking place in the real world. He argues that there has been a communication failure and that the pressure universities place on publishing has watered down the quality of work. He closes by saying that management failed because it was not focused on the issues of the day.

Title: An Industry-Occupational Forecast Incorporating Technological Change for Local/Regional Manpower Planning
Authors: John L. Iacobelli, Jan P. Muczyk
Affiliations: The Cleveland State University
Abstract: In this article the authors develop a model for forecasting future manpower demands in a variety of industries, in a variety of regions in the United States. They note that by knowing what the future demand will be in a given industry organizations can compare supply and demand and determine if labor shortages or surpluses are likely to occur. This information can in turn be used by policy makers to decrease gaps between supply and demand and improve conditions for both employers and employees. The authors discuss how improving technology affects the demand for labor and since this is a continual process being able to continually forecast labor demand will benefit employers immensely.

Title: Errata: Hypothesis of Work Behavior Revisited and an Extension
Participative Organization Diagnosis and Intervention Strategies: Developing Emergent Pragmatic Theories of Change
Authors: Noel M. Tichy, Harvey Hornstein, Jay N. Nisberg
Affiliations: Columbia University; Management Consultant
Abstract: A participative process for managers and consultants to build organization diagnostic and improvement models, called developing Emergent Pragmatic Theories of change, enables individuals to explicate their personal implicit models, and groups to combine personal models into shared group models which can be modified by exposure to relevant theory and research findings. This approach has been applied at General Motors and in training individuals.

Title: Creativity Techniques: Toward Improvement of the Decision Process
Affiliations: Southwest Missouri State University; U. S. Army
Abstract: Selected creativity techniques to improve the decision process are illustrated, their application to the decision process elaborated, and their contribution to organization performance hypothesized. Impediments to the use of creativity techniques are discussed and suggestions made to reduce the effects of those impediments.

Title: Models for Decision Making in Organizations and Some Contextual Variables Which Stipulate Optimal Use
Affiliations: Ohio State University
Abstract: Six organizational decision making models are described and critiqued. It is postulated that an optimum model can be selected by considering: dependencies among organizational units and layers, key tasks of each unit, performance assessment between adjacent layers, and environmental characteristics.

Title: Human Resource Accounting: A Measurement Perspective
Authors: Philip H. Mirvis, Barry A. Macy
Affiliations: The University of Michigan
Abstract: Human resource accounting is evaluated as a potential organizational measurement tool. Specifically, asset and cost models are examined in terms of reliability, validity, and usefulness. Beyond this evaluative perspective, examples are presented of a costing approach which may circumvent some of the identified measurement problems.

Title: Organization Development: A Review of Research Content and Research Design
Authors: Sam E. White, Terence R. Mitchell
Affiliations: University of Washington
Abstract: A review of research on Organization Development describes emphases in the OD field. A logical classification system for independent and dependent variables frequently employed in OD interventions is pro- posed for the continued theoretical and practical development of OD. Problems of methodology and research design are summarized and methods for improving effectiveness of OD research are suggested.

Title: The Effects and Effectiveness of Simulations in Business Policy Teaching Applications
Affiliations: University of Illinois, Chicago Circle
Abstract: The rigorous business policy gaming literature is reviewed against a criterion of business policy course content and teaching objectives. Gaming appears to support the objectives of strategy-making and goalsetting, and the study of personal and group factors in organizational decision making, while it seems to fail regarding the structuring elements and the appraising and controlling functions of business policy.

Title: Beyond Management and the Worker: The Institutional Function of Management
Affiliations: University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: Management's role in negotiating the organization's relationships with the environment has been neglected in theory and research. Strategies for managing interorganizational interdependence include: merger, joint ventures, cooptation, movement of personnel among organizations, regulation, and political activity. Institutional management activities can be explained using variables measuring dimensions of the organization's context.

Title: A Theoretical Analysis of the Impact of Task Scope on Employee Performance
Authors: Donald P. Schwab, L. L. Cummings
Affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison
Abstract: A model is presented linking task scope to employee motivation and performance. Emphasis is given to the importance of objective, environmental (versus psychological) conceptualizations of task scope. Psychological reactions to variations in task scope are depicted as dependent on intervening constructs. Through an expectancy model, a formulation of a task scope/performance relationship leads to a complex, situationally specific set of predictions. Additional refinements of the model are suggested.

Title: The Moral Codes of Executives: A Watergate-inspired Look at Barnard's Theory of Executive Responsibility
Affiliations: University of Wisconsin
Abstract: Chester Barnard's treatment of the functions of the executive climaxes in his largely neglected consideration of executive morality. A high priority needs to be given to the study of executive morality, in efforts to better understand executive behavior. Barnard provides a promising point of departure.

Title: Hypothesis Creation in Organizational Behavior Research
Affiliations: Oregon State University
Abstract: The field of organizational behavior has begun to place undue emphasis on hypothesis testing and thereby underemphasize hypothesis generation. After suggesting several reasons for this, this paper reviews how useful research ideas are discovered and the prerequisites for hypothesis creation, and then catalogues hypothesis generation. Suggested criteria for acting on new research ideas and questions are: extensity, professional encounter, mental experiments, and timing.

Title: International Management
Affiliations: St. Mary's University, San Antonio, Texas
Abstract: The article reviews several books pertaining to the topic of international management, including “Comparative Management and Economic Progress,” by Richard N. Farmer and Barry M. Richman, “Multinational Management,” by F. T. Haner, and “Management in the Industrial World,” by Frederick Harbison and Charles A. Myers.

Title: Organizational Behavior
Affiliations: Michigan State University
Abstract: The article reviews several books about organizational behavior, including “The Social Psychology of Organizations,” by Daniel Katz and Robert Kahn, “Individual Behavior and Group Achievement,” by Ralph M. Stogdill, and “Work and Motivation,” by Victor Vroom.

Title: Social Issues in Management
Affiliations: University of Pittsburgh
Abstract: The article reviews several books pertaining to social issues in management, including “Private Management and Public Policy,” by Lee E. Preston and James E. Post, “The Corporate Dilemma,” by Dow Votaw and S. Prakash Sethi, and “The Value Issue of Business,” by Alvar O. Elbing and Carol J. Elbing.

Title: Management Education and Development
Affiliations: The University of Akron
Abstract: The article reviews several books related to management education, including “The Case Method at the Harvard Business School,” edited by Malcolm P. McNair, “Training By Objectives: An Economic Approach to Management Training,” by George S. Odiorne, and “Dynamic Management Education,” by Allen A. Zoll.

Title: Management History Thought
Affiliations: School of Business Administration, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio 45056; Auburn University
Abstract: The article reviews several books related to management, including “The History of Management Thought,” by Claude George, “The Evolution of Management Thought,” by Daniel A. Wren, and “An Analysis of the Development of Management Thought in Europe and the United States,” by Brian Corbishley.

Title: One Sociologist's Reply to Wieland's Review Essay
Affiliations: Naval Postgraduate School
Abstract: George Wieland's survey of organization sociology texts represents a fundamental misunderstanding of the essential nature of sociology that distinguishes it from other academic disciplines and psychology in particular. Wieland's confusion probably represents the management field's thinking about organization sociology.

Title: That Word “Organization”
Affiliations: Longueville, Australia
Abstract: The article discusses the importance and various meanings of the word organization within the field of management science. For management education students, the author finds that the word is used in an aloof manner, most frequently in the United States. He attributes this occurrence to the different ways in which the word is used, including the way in which a company is managed and also as another word for the company itself. Other definitions also exist and the author argues that having so many meanings for one word dilutes its importance within the professional world.

Title: Modern Management Applied to Academic Decisions
Affiliations: Northwestern University
Abstract: Modern management has much to offer academic administrators who seek new ways to deal with complex institutional problems. There is a danger, however, in applying quantitative, mathematical tools to educational issues which are substantive and non-quantitative. Care should be exercised in applying such techniques as: cost-benefit analysis, linear programming, management by objectives and systems analysis.

Title: A Framework For Organization Assessment
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: A theoretical framework for analyzing the context, structure, process, and performance of complex organizations is developed. An attempt is made to (1) define and relate selected properties of macro and micro organization design and performance, (2) identify and compare different design patterns within a complex organization, and (3) explore how these differentiated patterns are linked as an intra-organizational network.

Title: Hypothesis of Work Behavior Revisited and an Extension
Affiliations: City University of New York
Abstract: Research generated by the Korman self-consistency motivational hypothesis is reviewed. Thirty-three studies are cited, with most field study evidence supportive. Laboratory research has resulted in mixed findings, but this may be due to methodological problems. An extension accounting for changes in motivational processes over time is proposed.

Title: Certain See.
Certain See
Affiliations: Naval Postgraduate School

Title: Achieving Corporate Social Responsibility
Affiliations: The University of Kansas
Abstract: Corporate social responsibility is defined as the serious attempt to solve social problems caused wholly or in part by the corporation. The problem concept is operationally defined, and social problems are distinguished from non-social problems. A method of social problem solution, based on the principles of applied behavior analysis, is demonstrated using an industrial accident reduction example.

Title: A Model for New Venture Initiation: A Discourse on Rapacity and the Independent Entrepreneur
Affiliations: The University of Alabama
Abstract: This conceptual model reflects a representative behavioral pattern for “the independent entrepreneur” re the venture construct. The model includes a five-stage sequence beginning with the pre-venture set up and extending through the anxious moments of re-negotiation or termination of the venture, resulting from the entrepreneur's rapacious act.

Title: Japanese Management — A Critical Review
Affiliations: California State University, Fullerton
Abstract: One must look beyond the behavioral aspects of the Japanese management system to the economic conditions which support the system to understand fully its contribution to Japan's economic recovery. Permanent employment (Nenko) has created a highly efficient dual wage and labor market system but it excludes two-thirds of the Japanese labor force from its benefits.

Title: Organizational Logic for Concurrent Government in Metropolitan Areas
Affiliations: San Diego State University
Abstract: In an urban environment of high diversity, governmental structure should be open and multinucleated to meet the performance criteria of efficiency and effectiveness. A case study of the Lakewood Plan illustrates that governmental structure is contingent upon environmental factors in the specific metropolitan area. The traditional “one best way” recommendation for consolidation assumes an oversimplification of the urban public economy.

Title: Editorial Comment.
